name: PT Sans
designer: Alexandra Korolkova, Olga Umpelova and Vladimir Yefimov
classification_notes: A humanist sans with enhanced legibility built for broad Cyrillic-minority-language coverage, sitting between conservative and contemporary in tone.
summary: The free, open-source humanist sans commissioned by the Russian government to cover every minority language written in Cyrillic.
description: PT Sans was commissioned by Rospechat to mark the 300th anniversary of Peter the Great's orthography reform, with a brief to cover almost every minority language of the Russian Federation alongside Latin. Basic weights are free under an open licence, while a Pro edition adds light, demi-bold, extra-bold and black weights across narrow, condensed and extra-condensed widths. A genuine workhorse rather than a display statement.
foundry_blurb: ParaType describes PT Sans as combining a traditional, conservative appearance with modern humanist sans trends, built for enhanced legibility and covering Latin and Cyrillic characters across almost all minority languages of the Russian Federation.

name: PT Serif
designer: Alexandra Korolkova, Olga Umpelova and Vladimir Yefimov
classification_notes: A transitional serif companion to PT Sans, sharing its brief for broad Cyrillic-Latin coverage rather than a distinct stylistic statement.
summary: The transitional serif half of the PT family, built for the same broad Cyrillic-Latin brief as PT Sans.
description: PT Serif pairs with PT Sans as part of the same government-commissioned project, offering a transitional serif with a caption cut for small print. The free basic set covers regular, italic and bold; the Pro edition adds 32 further styles including narrow and extended widths, small caps and text figures. Solid, legible, and built for print and documents rather than branding flair.
foundry_blurb: ParaType presents PT Serif as the serif companion to PT Sans, sharing its brief to support Latin and Cyrillic across the minority languages of the Russian Federation, with text figures and small caps in the commercial release.

name: PT Mono
designer: Alexandra Korolkova, Olga Umpelova and Vladimir Yefimov
classification_notes: A fixed-width companion to the PT family built specifically for programming use, placing it as a straightforward monospace.
summary: A free, open-source monospace for programming, completing the PT family alongside PT Sans and PT Serif.
description: PT Mono rounds out the PT project with a no-frills fixed-width face for code, matching its siblings' Latin and Cyrillic coverage. Two weights only, no italics, which is exactly what a programming font needs and nothing more.
foundry_blurb: ParaType positions PT Mono as a monospaced font intended for programming use, part of the free and open PT Fonts project alongside PT Sans and PT Serif.

name: Pragmatica
designer: Vladimir Yefimov, with Isabella Chaeva, Manvel Shmavonyan and Alexander Tarbeev
classification_notes: A Cyrillic neo-grotesque built on the structural logic of Univers, developed as an original Soviet-era adaptation rather than a licensed reissue.
summary: A long-running Cyrillic neo-grotesque in the Univers mould, one of ParaType's foundational originals.
description: Pragmatica was developed at ParaType in the late Soviet period as a Cyrillic neo-grotesque with the structural discipline of Univers, and has stayed in active use ever since. It now spans condensed widths, a slab-serif variant and a reworked Next edition. A dependable corporate workhorse rather than an expressive display face.
foundry_blurb: ParaType describes Pragmatica as one of its long-standing neo-grotesque families, originally released in 1989 and since expanded with condensed, slab and Next editions for contemporary use.

name: Newton
classification_notes: ParaType's Cyrillic-extended take on Times New Roman, originally released under the name TimesET, places it as a transitional text serif.
summary: ParaType's own take on Times New Roman, extended across Cyrillic, Greek, Armenian and Georgian.
description: Newton began life in 1990 as TimesET, an old-style-influenced reworking of Times New Roman built at ParaGraph for multi-script use. Its five styles cover books, reports and general office documents as readily as display and advertising. Unremarkable by design, which is exactly the point of a text serif this widely used.
foundry_blurb: ParaType describes Newton as based on Times New Roman by Stanley Morison and Victor Lardent, carrying many Old Style characteristics for better legibility, widely used in books, magazines and office documents.

name: Circe
classification_notes: A geometric sans with humanist qualities, expanded over time into rounded and contrast variants, places it as a contemporary geometric sans.
summary: A geometric sans with humanist warmth, one of ParaType's more contemporary originals with rounded and contrast siblings.
description: Circe pairs a geometric structure with softer, more humanist details across seven weights, with italics added some years after the initial release. The family has since grown to include Circe Rounded and Circe Contrast variants. A newer, more design-forward entry than ParaType's older Soviet-era workhorses.
foundry_blurb: ParaType describes Circe as a geometric sans-serif with humanist qualities, released in 2011 and later expanded with italic styles, plus Rounded and Contrast variants.

name: Literaturnaya
designer: Anatolii Shchukin, digitised by Lyubov Kuznetsova
classification_notes: A digitisation of a late-1930s Soviet book face based on Berthold's Latinskaya, this is a historical book/text serif rather than a contemporary design.
summary: The standard Cyrillic book face of the Soviet era, digitised by ParaType in 1996.
description: Literaturnaya was drawn at Poligraphmash in the late 1930s, based on Hermann Berthold's Latinskaya, and went on to set most Russian-language books from the 1950s to the 1990s. ParaType's 1996 digitisation keeps it available for anyone wanting that specific mid-century Soviet book aesthetic. A genuine historical workhorse rather than a revival for revival's sake.
foundry_blurb: ParaType notes Literaturnaya was designed at Poligraphmash in the late 1930s based on Berthold's Latinskaya, informally known as the favourite font of Russian typographers and the standard Cyrillic book face from the 1950s to the early 1990s.

name: Quant Antiqua
classification_notes: A revision of Literaturnaya developed at the same Polygraphmash bureau, this sits alongside its parent as a historical Cyrillic book serif.
summary: A 1989 revision of Literaturnaya, refining the same Soviet book-serif lineage.
description: Quant Antiqua was developed at the Polygraphmash type design bureau as a direct revision of Literaturnaya, keeping the same book-serif intentions with updated proportions. Three styles cover regular use without a heavier weight range. A closely related, lesser-known sibling to ParaType's more famous Cyrillic book faces.
foundry_blurb: ParaType credits Quant Antiqua to Lyubov Kuznetsova, designed at the Polygraphmash type design bureau in 1989 as a revision of Literaturnaya.

name: Lazurski
classification_notes: Based on a 1962 hot-metal design referencing early 16th-century Italian Renaissance type, this is classified as a renaissance-revival serif.
summary: A Cyrillic renaissance-revival serif based on Vadim Lazursky's 1962 hot-metal design.
description: Lazurski digitises book designer Vadim Lazursky's 1962 hot-metal typeface, itself a nod to early 16th-century Italian Renaissance letterforms. Vladimir Yefimov's 1984 digital version added demi and demi-italic weights. A quieter, more literary alternative to ParaType's plainer book faces.
foundry_blurb: ParaType describes Lazurski as based on a 1962 hot-metal typeface by Moscow book designer Vadim Lazurski, inspired by early 16th-century Italian Renaissance type, digitised at Polygraphmash in 1984 with added demi weights.
